Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Twenty-five years ago, Tane, a man of Oceania heritage born in California, stood on a crowded observation deck overlooking a foreign city square when the explosions began. The blast did not merely shatter the glass; it fixed him in place. He remembers the exact trajectory of the falling masonry, the way his left shoulder was pinned beneath a collapsed wooden railing, his knees bent at a sharp, unnatural angle, his breath trapped in a shallow rhythm that refused to deepen. For hours, he lay there, certain he would not be found. When he finally escaped, the memory arrived not as a fading echo but as a sharp, unrelenting recording. Over the months and years that followed, these memories refused to stay buried. They would force their way into his mind during quiet evenings, unbidden and absolute. The visual clarity never degraded—the precise crack in the pavement, the acrid taste of burnt wire, the heavy silence that followed the roar. When a siren wailed nearby or a car door slammed, his body would immediately tilt forward, his hips locking into that same trapped position, his muscles bracing against a weight that was no longer there. In the studio where he works as a painter, the details remain painfully sharp. He lives with the steady understanding that the world is a dangerous place, a place where sudden violence can fracture an ordinary day without warning. This certainty sits alongside his quiet conviction that he cannot rely on himself to stay safe, and that he cannot depend on other people to pull him free. These understandings do not feed into one another; they simply occupy his daily life. He keeps his emotions tightly controlled, measuring his voice and smoothing his features when contractors or suppliers stop by to discuss materials. He tells himself that showing any fluctuation would only invite uncertainty, so he holds his face still, his jaw set, until the visitor leaves. At the same time, he finds himself calling his sister or a former colleague after any sudden noise, asking them to confirm that he is okay, that he is safe, that nothing has happened. He repeats the question, listening for the steady certainty in their replies, until his shoulders finally drop. Going out has gradually become something he avoids, not as a sudden decision but as a series of small withdrawals over countless weekends. Over the first year, he began leaving the house only when absolutely necessary, timing his walks to avoid the rush of commuters. By the second year, he stopped answering calls from gallery organizers, telling himself he was too busy with studio work, when in truth the thought of entering a crowded room made his chest tighten. These habits formed side by side, each occupying a different corner of his routine. He prefers to stay within the familiar dimensions of his American home, where he knows the sound of the floorboards and the exact angle of the morning light. When he does step outside to collect a delivery, he walks with his weight forward, his gaze fixed on the street, his body preparing for a collapse that never comes. His hands, which once mixed colors with unhesitating grace, now tremble slightly when he reaches for his palette, a reminder of the stillness that once cost him his breath. His single life offers no one else to carry the weight of these patterns, so he manages them alone. Now, at seventy-one, Tane sits in the quiet of his living room, the phone resting heavy on the table beside him. He has come to believe that relying on himself is no longer possible, and waiting for others to reassure him has grown exhausting. What finally brought him to seek help was the quiet realization that his days have shrunk to a narrow corridor of waiting. He does not know what he hopes to find, only that he is tired of holding his breath, tired of bracing for the next impact, and tired of asking everyone around him to tell him he is still alive.
